what: MarketAxess runs an electronic marketplace for bonds. Corporate bonds have historically traded by telephone between dealers; MarketAxess lets institutional investors request prices from many dealers at once, and increasingly trade directly with each other, with the data and analytics that go around it.
customers: Asset managers, insurance companies, pension funds, hedge funds and the bank dealers who make markets in bonds, across US corporate credit, emerging markets, municipals and European credit.
money: Fees charged on the value of bonds traded through the platform.
Market data, analytics and trade processing services.
moat: A trading venue is a network: liquidity attracts liquidity, and the platform where the most participants already are is where the next participant wants to be. MarketAxess built that position in US investment-grade corporate credit over two decades, and its data business is a direct by-product — owning the trades means owning the price information that others need.
risks: Nine analysts average a $162.22 target against a $165.33 price — slightly below. Analysts rarely publish targets under the market, so this reflects genuine caution.
Tradeweb has been taking share in several of the products MarketAxess dominated, which is the first serious competitive pressure in years.
Revenue growth has slowed to a crawl: $817.1M in 2024 to $846.3M in 2025.
Trading volumes depend on credit market activity, which falls when markets are quiet, and pricing per trade has been under pressure.
The shares trade at about 20.3 times earnings and 6.7 times sales, which still prices in a dominant position.
opportunities: Net margin of about 29% and free cash flow of $352.4M on $871.6M of revenue show the economics of a trading venue clearly: once built, additional volume costs almost nothing to process.
Cash of $519.7M against $284.9M of debt gives a net cash position.
Electronic trading in bonds is still far less penetrated than in equities, so the structural shift from telephone to screen has a long way to run.
The data business grows with the trades and sells to participants who need pricing information whether or not they trade on the platform.
watch: Market share in US investment-grade and high-yield credit. This is a network business: share is the asset, and losing it is the only thing that genuinely matters here.
view: Electronic marketplaces are among the best businesses in finance when they win, and among the worst when they lose, because the thing being sold is liquidity and liquidity concentrates. Traders go where other traders are. That makes market share self-reinforcing in both directions: the leader’s position strengthens for years and then, if share starts moving, it moves faster than anyone expects. MarketAxess built a dominant position in US corporate credit over two decades, and the question now is which direction the self-reinforcement is running.

The evidence is not comfortable. Revenue growth has slowed to roughly 3.5%, Tradeweb has been taking share in several products MarketAxess used to own, and the nine analysts covering it have an average target slightly below the share price. Sell-side analysts are structurally reluctant to publish targets under the market; when a group of them does, it usually reflects modelling they cannot make work rather than caution for its own sake.

The quality of what remains is not in doubt. A 29% net margin and $352 million of free cash flow on $872 million of revenue is what a trading venue looks like once it is built — additional volume costs almost nothing to process, which is why these businesses are so profitable and so worth fighting for. The data business is a direct by-product: owning the trades means owning the price information, and that gets sold to people who never trade on the platform at all.

The structural argument in its favour is real and often overstated in its timing: bond trading is still far less electronic than equities, so the long-term shift from telephone to screen has years to run, and MarketAxess participates in that whatever happens to share. But participating in a growing market while losing share is a mediocre outcome, and at 20.3 times earnings you are paying for the dominant position rather than the participation. Market share in US investment-grade and high-yield credit is the only number that settles this, and it is reported monthly.
bull: Electronic penetration of bond trading keeps rising while MarketAxess holds its share, and a 29% margin network business compounds with volume at almost no incremental cost.
bear: Tradeweb keeps taking share in the products MarketAxess dominated, growth stays near zero, and a network business losing its network repricess fast.
